power and jurisdiction to supervise and regulate the rates and service of every public utility

Commission must determine a fair rate of return that the utility should be allowed the
opportunity to earn after recovery of the expenses of utility operations. The legal standards
for this determination are set forth in Federal Power Comm’n v. Hope Natural Gas Co.,
320 U.S. 591, 602-03 (1944) (Hope) and Bluefield Water Works & Improvement Co.
v.
Pub. Serv. Comm’n of West Virginia, 262 U.S. 679, 692-93 (1923) (Bluefield).
Bluefield holds that:
What annual rate will constitute just compensation
depends upon many circumstances,
and must be
determined by the exercise of a fair and enlightened
judgment, having regard to
all relevant facts.
A
public utility is entitled to such rates as will permit it
to earn a return on the value of the property which it
employs for the convenience of the public equal to
that generally being made at the same time and in the
same general part of the country on investments in
other business undertakings which are attended by
corresponding risks and uncertainties; but it has no
constitutional right to profits such as are realized or
anticipated
in
highly
profitable
enterprises
or

ventures.

financial

enable it to raise the money necessary for the proper
discharge of its public duties. A rate of return may be

This Commission and the South Carolina courts have consistently applied the
principles set forth in Bluefield and Hope. In Southern Bell Tel. & Tel. Co.
v. Pub. Serv.
Comm'n (Southern Bell), the South Carolina Supreme Court, quoting Hope, held: “Under
the statutory standard of ‘just and reasonable’ it is the result reached not the method
employed which is controlling
.
.
. The ratemaking process under the Act, 1.e., the fixing of
‘just and reasonable’ rates, involves the balancing of investor and the consumer interests.”
270 S.C. 590, 596-97, 244 S.E.2d 278, 281 (quoting Hope, 320 U.S. at 602-03).
This Commission must exercise its dual responsibility of permitting utilities an
opportunity to earn a reasonable return on the property the utility has devoted to serving
the public while also protecting customers from rates that are so excessive as to be unjust
or unreasonable by ‘“(a) Not depriving investors of the opportunity to earn reasonable
returns on the funds devoted to such use as that would constitute a taking ofprivate property
without just compensation [and] (b) Not permitting rates which are excessive.” Southern
Bell, 270 S.C. at 605, 244 S.E.2d at 286 (Ness, J. concurring and dissenting). Ultimately,
this balancing act takes place within the context of a utility setting forth proposed rates
—
pursuant to Title 58, Chapter 27, Article 7 of the South Carolina Code of Laws
— for the
purpose of the utility receiving revenue sufficient to yield a reasonable return.

Commission Decision
The baseline for establishing an appropriate rate of return on common equity are
established by the decisions of the United States Supreme Court in Bluefield and Hope,
which establish that the ROE should be set at a level (1) commensurate with returns on
investments in other firms having corresponding risks; (ii) sufficient to assure confidence
in DESC’s financial integrity; and (111) sufficient to maintain DESC’s creditworthiness and
ability to attract capital on reasonable terms.
The
Commission is the fact finder in rate proceedings and must balance the interests
of the using and consuming public with that of the utility appearing before it. Additionally,
the Commission’s determination of a fair rate of return must be based on reliable and
probative evidence in the record. As a result, this Commission is bound by the parameters
of evidence in the record, and it hereby carefully evaluates the evidence submitted in this
case as to what ROE the Company should be authorized the opportunity to earn.
In this case, after consideration of the record, the Commission concludes that it is
just, reasonable, and a fair balancing of the interests of the Company and its customers to
approve the ROE of 9.99% as set out in the Revenue Requirement Stipulation. An ROE of
9.99% is supported by the record before the Commission, as it is within the range of ROE
estimates recommended by Witness Baudino. The Commission gives significant weight to
the compromise of the Revenue Requirement Stipulating Parties in reaching the Revenue
Requirement Stipulation, and DESC witnesses’ testimony in support thereof. As such, an
ROE of 9.99% is a reasonable compromise in this proceeding.
